stories.title: Colt DCS and RMZ commence construction on third Mumbai data center
stories.summary: Colt Data Centre Services (Colt DCS), a global provider of AI-ready, hyperscale and large enterprise data centers, and RMZ, one of India’s largest privately owned real assets platform, have announced the commencement of construction of Mumbai 3, the third data center of Colt DCS in the city. This will be an AI-ready facility located at […]
stories.content:
Colt Data Centre Services (Colt DCS), a global provider of AI-ready, hyperscale and large enterprise data centers, and RMZ, one of India’s largest privately owned real assets platform, have announced the commencement of construction of Mumbai 3, the third data center of Colt DCS in the city. This will be an AI-ready facility located at the operator’s Navi Mumbai Campus that will deliver 64 MW upon completion.

In a press release, Colt DCS said that Mumbai 3 is being developed as part of Colt DCS and RMZ’s joint venture announced in 2024, to invest US$ 1.7 billion in the Indian data center market. Ground preparation began in December 2025, and construction is now underway following the signing of the facility’s first hyperscale customer.

“The nature of data center demand is evolving rapidly, with customers requiring larger deployments, higher rack densities and infrastructure capable of supporting increasingly intensive AI workloads. Mumbai 3 is designed to address these needs, further strengthening our Navi Mumbai Campus as a scalable and future-ready digital infrastructure platform,” said Pratap Mane, Country Head, India, Colt DCS.

“The next wave of digital growth will be driven by infrastructure that brings together scale, resilience, and speed to market. At Mumbai 3, we are developing a future-ready campus designed to enable hyperscalers and neo-cloud providers to scale seamlessly as their capacity and computing needs evolve,” said Deepak Chhabria, President, RMZ Infrastructure.

Mumbai 3 will join existing data centers Mumbai 1 and Mumbai 2 at the Navi Mumbai Campus, which currently supports large enterprise and cloud workloads. The campus has the potential to deliver up to 148 MW of capacity at full development and, upon completion, Mumbai 3 will increase the site’s operational capacity to 86 MW.

Mumbai 3 has been designed to support AI workloads and high-density compute deployments, delivering 64 MW of secured contracted power, supported by a hybrid cooling architecture that combines traditional air cooling with direct liquid-to-chip cooling. The facility will also benefit from a 220kV GIS substation located on campus, providing high levels of resilience and scalability, alongside carrier-neutral connectivity with access to high-capacity fiber routes.

Sustainability and long-term community impact have been central considerations in the development of Mumbai 3. The facility will operate using 100% renewable energy and has been designed with a closed-loop cooling system, enabling near-zero wastewater from the cooling process.

stories.title: Greece proposes new rules for data center electricity connections
stories.summary: Greece’s Ministry of Environment and Energy has opened a public consultation on legislation introducing new rules for electricity market operations and data center connections. Under the proposed framework data center investors would be required to cover the full cost of connecting their facilities to the electricity grid, including any necessary upgrades to the power system […]
stories.content:
Greece’s Ministry of Environment and Energy has opened a public consultation on legislation introducing new rules for electricity market operations and data center connections. Under the proposed framework data center investors would be required to cover the full cost of connecting their facilities to the electricity grid, including any necessary upgrades to the power system resulting directly from their connection.

According to a press release, new data centers would also have to source at least 60 percent of their annual electricity consumption from renewable energy sources. The draft bill introduces a financial guarantee of € 200,000 (US$ 244,000) per MW of requested capacity. The measure is intended to discourage applications from investors whose projects are not sufficiently developed but could otherwise reserve available grid capacity.

Investors seeking to connect projects to the transmission system operated by the Independent Power Transmission Operator (IPTO) would also face financial viability checks based on specific turnover requirements.

The legislation would tighten the investment and environmental criteria applicants must meet before receiving a Definitive Connection Offer. It also proposes establishing a data center register under the Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY) to monitor sector development and improve transparency.

Separately, the draft legislation sets out rules for the operation, maintenance and monitoring of privately owned renewable energy networks, including requirements concerning infrastructure security and environmental protection.

The proposed measures come as authorities seek to manage growing electricity demand from data centers while addressing constraints on available grid capacity and the costs associated with connecting new large-scale consumers.

The consultation runs from October 10 to October 24, 2026, and the proposed legislation incorporates EU Directive 2024/1711, which amends Directives 2018/2001 and 2019/944, and includes additional provisions on the development of energy infrastructure.

stories.title: Data centre builders pre-order generators two years ahead
stories.summary: Data centre builders are ordering generators two years in advance, committing to suppliers before designs are final. This prioritises speed of delivery over cost due to shortages of power equipment and skilled labour for AI-era projects.
stories.content:
Data centre builders are now ordering generators two years ahead and committing to suppliers before final designs are complete, according to speakers at Capacity Europe 2026. This shift places speed of delivery above cost, driven by shortages of power equipment and skilled labour.The "Scaling Under Scarcity: Delivering Projects Amid Shortages" panel on 14 October highlighted that the industry's traditional focus on negotiating the lowest price has changed to securing manufacturing slots.Miriam van Kooperen, senior director, supply chain at Greenscale, noted that high-voltage transformers, gas-insulated switchgear, and generator engines are currently in short supply. She warned that the gap between rapid AI development and available manufacturing capacity is widening.Ozgur Duzgunoglu, head of engineering and design at Telehouse, confirmed that generators can take two years to arrive, with high-voltage transformers requiring 12 to 18 months. He described a situation where his team faced a Friday deadline to order generators for a two-year delivery.Nelson Pinto de Magalhaes, director, PMO and procurement at Start Campus, stated that long-lead equipment can be managed through early commitments. However, he added that coordinating equipment, installers, and commissioning teams for simultaneous arrival remains challenging.Panellists described a fundamental change in contracting with suppliers. Van Kooperen explained that operators now secure capacity without knowing exact specifications, agreeing on preferred vendors and broad design freeze dates.Start Campus has integrated procurement and design teams, with Pinto de Magalhaes stating, "Procure first, design around it" is a company mantra. He reframed procurement around time rather than money, noting that customers judge operators on meeting the ready-for-service (RFS) date.Duzgunoglu agreed that designers and contractors are scarce, alongside the difficulty of bringing grid power to sites on time. He noted that cost sometimes becomes secondary to hitting the RFS date.Prefabrication, such as off-site manufactured coolant distribution units, is now common for time savings, Duzgunoglu said. Justin Ryburn, field CTO and VP of global solutions engineering at Kentik, cited a US data centre customer running generators continuously until grid power arrives.Oracle has issued a force majeure notice for Project Jupiter, its Stargate campus in New Mexico, due to potential power supply delays for its 2028 start. Panellists anticipate power and skilled labour shortages, particularly in mechanical, electrical, and plumbing (MEP) trades, to remain bottlenecks for the foreseeable future.

stories.title: Construction inflation pressures data center project viability
stories.summary: Rising construction costs, now 3 per cent to 6 per cent annually, are challenging data center project viability, according to JLL. Projects require secured power access and committed anchor tenants to absorb these higher expenses.
stories.content:
Annual data center construction cost escalation has reached 3 per cent to 6 per cent, up from 2 per cent to 3 per cent before 2020, JLL reported in its Global Construction Costs Index 2026.The real estate services firm forecasts another 3.1 per cent to 4.2 per cent increase in global tender prices in 2027. These forecasts apply broadly to construction, not solely the data center sector.Data center developers can pass higher construction costs to tenants only when projects have secured power access, committed customers, and a credible path to delivery, JLL stated.Matthew Giddings, executive director of technical services with JLL’s Data Centers and Critical Environments team, noted that stronger market fundamentals do not automatically protect individual projects.“The economics break down when costs outpace contracted revenue or power delays postpone income while financing costs continue to accumulate,” Giddings told Data Center Knowledge.He added that higher asset values alone cannot close that gap. This risk is most acute for speculative campuses without anchor tenants, projects with uncertain power delivery, and developments tied to fixed-rent agreements.Older facilities being repositioned for AI workloads may also face difficult economics if upgrades become too extensive.“Strong demand supports the market, but it does not make every project viable,” Giddings said. Developers should reassess projects when rising capital costs erode expected returns, utility schedules slip, or tenant demand no longer supports planned capacity, he explained.Reduced power availability and delays in anchor-tenant commitments are also signs that a project may need to be reworked.One way to manage this risk is through phased construction. This aligns spending with confirmed electricity supply and customer demand, limiting capital commitment before fundamentals are in place.
### Labor and Procurement Challenges

Skilled electrical and mechanical trades are creating the greatest cost and schedule challenges, Giddings said. This includes electricians, high-voltage specialists, pipefitters, and advanced cooling technicians.“Controls, commissioning, and startup teams have also become critical bottlenecks, as their availability often determines when a completed facility can be placed into service,” he noted.Competition for utility and substation construction crews is also intensifying, adding risks beyond the data center site. Giddings recommended bringing in trade partners early and testing project schedules against real workforce availability.Standardized designs, off-site prefabrication, and phased construction can reduce peak labor requirements. In remote markets, developers may need to offer housing, transportation, and travel incentives to attract workers.Long lead times for critical equipment have pushed many developers to place orders earlier. However, this can create problems if tenant requirements shift, especially as AI infrastructure evolves.“The key is to secure manufacturing capacity early without freezing every design decision,” Giddings said.Developers should reserve production slots for transformers, switchgear, generators, and cooling equipment. They need flexibility to modify specifications before fabrication begins, advancing orders with validated tenant requirements and clear decision deadlines.This approach is crucial as operators account for shifting rack densities and growing interest in liquid cooling. Modular power and cooling systems, built-in expansion capacity, and design provisions for liquid cooling help facilities adapt.“Early procurement protects the schedule, while flexible design protects the long-term value of the asset,” Giddings stated.Retrofitting older facilities can offer faster delivery and lower upfront costs, especially with available power, structural capacity, and reusable infrastructure. These advantages can disappear if major mechanical upgrades, higher electrical distribution capacity, heavier floor loading, or large-scale liquid-cooling retrofits are needed.“The economics ultimately depend on how much existing infrastructure can be retained while still meeting current and future performance requirements,” Giddings concluded.

stories.title: NITI Aayog frames data center assessment for states
stories.summary: NITI Aayog released a framework for states to assess data center projects, aiming to ensure sustainable growth. The framework evaluates resource needs such as electricity, water, and land.
stories.content:
NITI Aayog has released a framework to help states evaluate data center projects based on infrastructure availability, resource needs, and economic benefits. The "Data Centre Evaluation Framework to Help States Plan for Sustainable Growth" calls on states to assess electricity, water, land, and supporting infrastructure. It aims to support informed decision-making by states.The government's think tank proposed five pillars for project evaluation. These include power and energy, water and cooling, site selection and environmental sustainability, economic and strategic value, and policy and implementation.States must assess if their electricity grids can meet data center demand, accounting for future expansion and needed upgrades. The report also asks states to evaluate long-term water availability, considering existing users like households and farmers. It recommends preparing a 20-30 year seasonal catchment water balance covering surface and groundwater.The framework suggests designating data-center-ready zones. This involves verifying land title, permitted use, zoning, and expansion headroom. It prioritises renewable-energy-rich zones with available connectivity and pre-assessed grid and water readiness.States are also urged to assess the net economic contribution of projects against public support offered to developers. This includes incentives for land, infrastructure, and electricity. The framework encourages linking incentives to measurable outcomes such as project commissioning, renewable energy use, and local procurement. It also calls for a time-bound digital single-window mechanism for project approvals. States should publish an approval matrix listing required clearances, authorities, processing times, and fees.

stories.title: Mitsubishi Heavy & Ingeteam team up on US data centres
stories.summary: Rising AI electricity demand is pushing US data centre operators to seek more reliable power systems as the firms plan broader integration work.
stories.content:
Fri, 16th Oct 2026 (Today)
Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Ingeteam have formed a strategic partnership focused on power solutions for US data centres, covering distribution, integration and joint development.

The agreement targets energy infrastructure for facilities handling AI computing workloads, where operators face rising electricity demand and more complex power quality issues.

Under a memorandum of understanding, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries plans to expand the availability of Ingeteam's power conversion systems and related software in the US data centre market. The companies will also examine how those technologies can be integrated into Mitsubishi Heavy Industries' broader energy infrastructure offering.

The partnership will also assess potential collaboration in medium-voltage distribution technology, energy management systems and other equipment for high-density computing environments.

### Rising demand

AI computing has increased power requirements across data centres as operators deploy denser racks and larger hardware clusters. That has intensified scrutiny of how electricity is supplied and managed within facilities, particularly where fluctuating AI workloads can affect power quality.

Operators are looking for ways to improve the efficiency, reliability and scalability of distribution systems. Harmonic distortion, voltage imbalance and longer waits for grid interconnection have also increased interest in architectures designed to work more closely with the grid.

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries will bring experience in integrated power, cooling and energy management to the partnership. Ingeteam's contribution centres on power electronics, power conversion, control and automation systems, and digital tools.

Mitsubishi Heavy Industries also highlighted its North American service footprint through Concentric, which supports its work on large industrial and infrastructure projects. Ingeteam's portfolio includes electrical generators, battery energy storage systems, power quality and grid stability technologies, and EMS/SCADA platforms.

### US focus

The alliance will initially focus on the United States, where data centre development has accelerated alongside investment in AI infrastructure. The companies described the move as a first step and said they would continue working with other technology partners as they develop products and systems for the market.

Shin Gomi, Senior General Manager, Data Centre & Energy Management Department at Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, said the issue for operators has moved beyond access to electricity alone.

"The challenge is no longer just securing power. It is delivering high-quality, reliable power to support AI workloads," said Shin Gomi, Senior General Manager, Data Centre & Energy Management Department at MHI.

"Ingeteam's depth in power electronics and power conversion strengthens our ability to deliver complete, reliable solutions for our U.S. data center customers developing AI Data Centres," Gomi said.

For Ingeteam, the partnership offers a route into a fast-growing segment of US infrastructure spending tied to AI-related data centre expansion.

"This alliance lets Ingeteam bring our power electronics and grid expertise to U.S. data centers alongside a partner with deep systems-engineering capability. Together, we can provide a bridge between the electric grid and next-generation AI infrastructure, enabling customers to scale computing capacity while maintaining reliability and efficiency," said Adolfo Rebollo, Chief Executive Officer at Ingeteam.

The agreement reflects a broader push by equipment suppliers and industrial groups to position themselves around the build-out of AI data centres, where demand for electricity, cooling and control systems is rising alongside computing density. Potential future areas of work include advanced medium-voltage distribution and energy management systems for sites with large, variable power loads.

Ingeteam employs more than 4,000 people across 15 countries, while Mitsubishi Heavy Industries operates in sectors including energy, infrastructure, industrial machinery, aerospace and defence.

stories.title: Market sell-off, rising rates test AI data centre deal boom
stories.summary: Pulled listings signal tougher funding conditions; investors question valuations as borrowing costs rise

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
Pulled listings signal tougher funding conditions; investors question valuations as borrowing costs rise

\[HONG KONG\] A market sell-off is forcing companies driving the global artificial intelligence boom to delay fundraising plans or pay more for capital as investors demand proof that they can absorb rising interest rates and computing-power costs.

The shift comes as investors reassess whether the companies racing to build the infrastructure underpinning AI can generate returns that justify soaring spending on computing power, land and energy.

In the past week alone, as AI-related stocks have weakened and the debt of data-centre operator CoreWeave has slumped towards distressed prices, listings for a Blackstone-backed AirTrunk Reit, Nvidia-backed Firmus and SoftBank-backed SB Energy have either been pulled or paused.

The increased scrutiny is not derailing investment in the sector, analysts said, but it is forcing investors to distinguish more sharply between business models and levels of execution risk.

“The conversation has shifted from growth at any cost to a much sharper focus on quality,” said Harry Evans, a partner at law firm Freshfields.

He added that deal activity could hold up through next year, thanks to a strong pipeline.

Recent listing setbacks, however, show investors are becoming more discerning about valuations, leverage and business models.

Mergers and acquisitions involving Asian data centres is still on track for a record year, reaching US$21.3 billion on Tuesday (Oct 13), Dealogic data showed. This is more than double the US$10 billion recorded in all of 2025.

Debt financing has also remained strong, with syndicated loans and bond issuance totalling US$22.3 billion so far this year.

Equity capital market fundraising for the sector, however, is down, at US$5.4 billion so far this year, a 4.6 per cent drop from the same period in 2025.

“General thoughts with IPOs (initial public offerings) are that they often seek ‘hype’, as they’re largely looking for oversubscription,” said Nicholas Tuan, director of Asia-Pacific advisory services at real estate services firm Savills.

“There may not be fundamental asset value when you peel it all back.”

Firmus, which had aimed to raise US$5 billion in what would have been Australia’s second-largest stock market listing, struggled to convince investors that it could deliver on ambitious revenue projections while carrying about US$30 billion of debt.

Nuclear services company Holtec cited a “perfect storm”, driven mainly by uncertainty around data-centre demand, when it pulled its US listing last month.

## Higher rates test valuations

Higher borrowing costs are at the heart of the new scrutiny.

Benchmark 10-year US Treasury yields posted their sharpest quarterly rise this century in September, prompting investors to take a closer look at whether projected revenues can support growing debt burdens, bankers said.

Gary Goh, CEO of Sprint DC Consulting, an Asia-Pacific data centre consultancy firm based in Kuala Lumpur, warned that higher financing costs could lead to sharp valuation corrections.

Valuations can vary widely depending on whether they are based on existing customer contracts or future projections, and whether capital expenditure requirements are fully reflected, said a banker who advises data centre investors.

“There is not remotely enough data centres built for the demand,” said the banker, who was not authorised to speak publicly. “Investors are still going in but the question is at what valuation.”

Investors are also paying closer attention to execution risks.

Beyond higher power and water costs, developers face growing opposition in some markets over electricity use, noise and environmental concerns, adding to regulatory uncertainty around new projects.

Securing suitable land and power supplies is becoming more difficult in some jurisdictions, said a person at a US-based firm that invests in Asian data centre platforms, adding that the company had tightened its underwriting criteria because of geopolitical and policy risks.

To be sure, major transactions are still moving ahead.

Singapore-based DayOne is expected to go public as soon as November, seeking to raise up to US$5 billion, Reuters reported in September. DayOne did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

AirTrunk, despite postponing a planned real estate investment trust listing, is nearing a deal to sell its Johor data centre in Malaysia to a group of investors including local pension fund Kwap at a valuation of about US$1 billion, according to two people familiar with the matter.

Bain Capital has also received final bids for at least 40 per cent of its pan-Asian platform Bridge Data Centres in a deal that could value the business at around US$5 billion, two sources said.

AirTrunk’s backer Blackstone and Bain Capital declined to comment. Kwap said it was not in a position to comment.

Still, investors are likely to differentiate between established wholesale operators with long-term customer commitments and stable revenue, and higher-risk “neoclouds” and “AI-campus builders”, said John Dinsdale, chief analyst at TechInsights.

“The question for investors is less whether demand will expand than which business models and companies will be best placed to capture that growth sustainably.” REUTERS

stories.title: DigiCo signs 71MW lease for Sydney data center with unnamed tech firm
stories.summary: Deal includes reallocation of 20MW of existing contracted capacity
stories.content:
DigiCo Infrastructure REIT has secured a major customer for its Sydney data center in Australia.

The ASX-listed firm announced this week that it has signed a 15-year contract for 71MW of capacity at its SYD1 facility in Sydney with an unnamed global technology firm, backed by "investment-grade credit support."

The facility, which is set to reach 88MW once current upgrades and expansions are complete, is now 100 percent leased.

The contract includes the reallocation of 20MW of existing contracted capacity to the new customer. The remaining 17MW of SYD1 capacity is leased to co-location customers.

DigiCo is in the midst of expanding the SYD site, set to nearly double its capacity. The company said the first 10MW of the SYD1 Expansion is expected to be energized and income-producing in late Q4 FY27, with the balance delivered progressively over FY28, aligned to customer requirements.

Simon Mitchell, co-head and CFO of DGT, said: “Execution of the 71MW contract at SYD1 is a key milestone for DGT, taking the site to 100 percent contracted across 88MW of total capacity. The 15-year agreement with a global technology firm provides long -term earnings visibility, supported by investment-grade credit backing. It validates the quality of our infrastructure and strengthens the quality of cash flows from our portfolio."

Investment manager HMC Capital acquired Global Switch’s Australian business, comprising a two-building facility in the Ultimo area of Sydney, in 2024. The company then launched and floated DigiCo Real Estate Investment Trust, a new company to hold its data center assets, including the Sydney facility.

“When we acquired SYD1, our business plan was to fully lease and develop the site to 88MW over five years, and we now expect to reach that milestone well ahead of our original plan," Mitchell added.

stories.title: NTT deploys Nvidia GPU test cluster at Munich 2 data center
stories.summary: Allows customers to test AI applications on Nvidia Blackwell hardware
stories.content:
NTT Global Data Centres has deployed an Nvidia GPU cluster at its Munich 2 data center.

According to the company, the cluster provides clients with a “real-world environment” where they can test how their AI applications will perform at scale before investing in broad deployments themselves.

Unlike a traditional AI demonstration or innovation lab, the cluster – which NTT has dubbed AI Factory Munich – allows customers to evaluate AI workloads against the infrastructure, security, data, governance and operational requirements they will face in production.

In a post on LinkedIn, Anne-Sophie Lotgering, CEO Europe, NTT, said that Nvidia and Dell provided the infrastructure whilst Red Hat and Mistral AI worked with the company on the platform and the model. The cluster is comprised of Nvidia Blackwell GPUs interconnected via Nvidia Spectrum-X Ethernet technology, with servers and storage provided by Dell’s AI Factory, with Nvidia offering.

“Every leader I speak to wants AI they own, control and trust. At NTT Data's AI factory Munich, they can run their own applications and data in a production data center, on their terms, before they commit to deployment. It‘s the difference between a slide and a decision,” said Graham Clarke, managing director, global private and sovereign AI, NTT Data.

Located in the German town of Unterschleißheim outside Munich, Bavaria, NTT’s 6,300 sqm (67,813 sq ft) Munich 2 campus consists of two buildings offering 14MW of critical IT load.

stories.title: Ensuring uptime, insuring downtime
stories.summary: Can the insurance industry keep up with data center growth?
stories.content:
Imagine there’s a real estate sector growing globally at a CAGR of 14 percent, with the promise of near-guaranteed returns, stable rent-based cash flows, and enough demand that supply can barely keep up. Investing in such a fertile field would be a no-brainer. In reality, you don’t need to imagine. That fertile land and its promise exists in today’s data center market.

While, in some cases, data centers are already delivering on this dream, no investment is without risk. And, from the pressure of high uptime standards, to uncertainty around AI returns, or even the threat of destruction from enemies and saboteurs, data centers are facing increasing and varied risks across the globe.

The obvious and traditional choice to mitigate that risk is insurance. But with data center hype reaching a fever pitch, and alchemical growth following, the slow-moving insurance markets are struggling to keep up.

In their reticence to miss out on a sure thing, those involved in data center construction and operation are leaving themselves somewhat exposed to new avenues of loss and risk, as an insurance protection gap emerges in the industry shield wall, leaving investors exposed to a hail of jeopardy.

## As above, so below

The huge investments in AI infrastructure over the past few years have given all sectors serving the data center industry a significant boost. Insurance is no slouch here, seeing significant growth in global re/insurance for data centers.

Demand for this infrastructure is nowhere near slowing yet, and there are still further opportunities for insurers to carve an even bigger parcel of land in the data center market.

Charles-Marie Delpuech, insurance analyst at S&P Global Ratings, estimates a total insurable asset base of over $2 trillion in the data center sector.

“Based on our projection and average annual investments of $300 billion, this asset base could double in six to seven years,” he adds.

In a recent report on insurable risks for data centers, S&P Global Ratings says that demand for data center insurance coverage could generate $10bn in new premiums in 2026. The research firm contextualizes this against another large insurance market, global aviation, which has annual premiums of around $5 billion.

Hyperscale data centers today are significantly larger and more complex than the more traditional deployments that pre-dated the emergence of generative AI and machine learning. This presents a wealth of opportunities for insurers, who will be able to offer services to the entire ecosystem that goes into the construction of such a data center. Developers, builders, utilities providers, investors, and lenders will all have insurance needs going into a project.

As hyperscalers continue to increase their capex, which is forecast to reach $700bn in 2026, they are looking to external funding sources. Delpuech says these investors may require high insured limits, and will likely continue to drive demand for insurance, both to protect assets or cash flows, such as rental income.

However, with such a high level of demand, some insurers are facing more supply than they can handle. One example of this is insurance firm Parametrix, which provides a range of insurance products, including service-level agreement insurance for data centers. Jonathan Hatzor, co-founder and CEO of Parametrix, argues that the insurance market has been slow to adapt.

“You have a risk that is growing, and usually when you have that, the insurance market is there to try to minimize this risk,” he explains. “But in data centers, we still see a lot of demand but not enough supply of insurance, which is also increasing the entire risk factor.”

Hatzor uses the example of investors offering a loan to purchase GPUs for a data center project: “Think about a debt provider or investors that provide a $10bn loan or equity to buy GPUs. The insurance market can not provide a $10bn property coverage for GPUs.

“There is no historical example of insuring properties with equipment worth $10bn inside of it,” he says. “It’s not just the risk that investors are concerned about; it’s also the fact that the insurance market is slow to adapt.”

He jokes: “It’s not just because we’re dinosaurs or because insurance companies are very old, there’s just no historical records of how resilient those GPUs are.”

Hatzor adds that the insurance market needs to catch up and offer a proper insurance ecosystem in order to really “unleash the potential” of the data center sector.

Despite its slowness, the insurance market is rising to meet growing demand on multiple fronts. Delpuech says insurers are increasing available capacity or adapting their insurance products to match.

“Nonetheless, as we may expect from the insurance industry, before taking additional risks we expect underwriting standards and discipline to remain the focus,” he explains.

Many data center companies today are covered by existing general business insurance, but data center-specific exposures are necessitating more defined coverage. When it comes to these specialized coverages, insurers will remain cautious about their offerings, Delpuech says, and in the meantime, hyperscalers may need to look to self-insure uncovered risks.

One way of doing this, for example, is with captive insurance – a form of self-insurance whereby a company creates its own licensed insurance subsidiary, allowing them to better manage hard-to-place risks and their associated costs.

Corroborating Hatzor’s earlier point, Delpuech states that data center projects now have coverage limits that go “beyond historical larger infrastructure projects like bridges and tunnels, which could have required a maximum $5-$10bn in coverage.”

“Some commercial insurers are now offering per-risk limits in the low single-digit billions for data center exposures, still short of the exposure that is coming to the market.”

But he adds: “Collaboration will be key. Given the size and complexity of these projects, insurers are increasingly working together to share risks, and we have seen many broker-led facilities increasing their aggregate capacity in recent months.”

## Always on, sometimes covered

Another growing avenue for data center insurance is SLA insurance. Downtime risk is a direct threat to operational incomes and returns because of the various financial penalties that are built into tenancy agreements.

SLA insurance is a solution to this, turning the volatility of an SLA into an insurable risk. Parametrix says solutions such as this are providing the predictability that will attract the capital required to build out the data center sector.

Hatzor says that, in the past, operators were simply trying to convince investors that downtime is extremely rare, especially in a Tier III or Tier IV data center. But with growing interest in the sector from investors, those coming from more predictable asset classes, wanted something more stable.

Institutional buyers are therefore increasingly requiring SLA insurance as part of M&A and refinancing deals.

These sorts of risks and exposures – downtime, power dependency, or operational disruption – are increasingly becoming a focus for insurers as opportunities to provide more coverage. These risks are becoming as challenging, or in some cases more challenging, than risks associated with physical assets.

However, when it comes to AI infrastructure, SLA insurance is still an emerging service. Delpuech predicts that this type of insurance will become an even bigger topic in the coming years, as the facilities being built today start operation.

“Insurers already have a strong presence in the typical data centers property insurance space,” he explains, “what we are seeing is the new complexity and scale of the hyperscale data centers where we expect insurers will expand for risk and limits they are comfortable with.”

“The reality is that the demand for insurance that has not been historically provided is only starting to come.”

Downtime is tricky to insure, especially when you consider interconnectedness with other data centers. Some specialized insurers will likely look to increase their capacity to meet these insurance demands. But, in some cases, it is likely that larger data center operators will look to cover these exposures with captive insurance systems.

In any case, no single insurer will be able to absorb all of the risks associated with data centers, which are in and of themselves collaborative structures. It is likely that insurers will look to partner to share the risk associated with data centers. S&P Global Ratings says it expects collaborative structures to “play an increasingly central role in scaling up the insurance market’s response,” and that alternative capital will start providing capacity as the market develops.”

## Exposures and risks

Common concentration risks can often simply come from the geographical footprint of the data center, which can often mean exposure to natural disasters, especially if there are many high-value assets concentrated in a single location.

For example, a recent report from MS Amlin found that half of planned US data centers, which are now increasingly being built in the south of the country, are at risk from severe convective storms, hurricanes, winterstorms, and earthquakes.

Delpuech says it is “pretty standard” for the industry to be able to locate and accumulate property exposure as they would do across all of their insured properties, not just data centers.

However, building a data center requires integration of multiple stakeholders: the end-user, developers, builders, utilities providers, and investors. With so many affected parties in the same space, and as this complexity increases with more complex data centers, providing multiple insurance products to participants in the same data center can cause concentration. Insurers will need to be careful to avoid concentration and aggregation risk.

Delpuech says data quality and tracking will be important in avoiding and dealing with these exposures.

In order to deal with more specialized risks, specialized commercial insurers generally take the lead on data center projects, Delpuech says, with “great expertise” in engineering and construction risk.

“The traditional property risk where most capacity is deployed is well understood by the industry,” Delpuech notes, “where it becomes more complex is everything related to business interruption or cyber. This is where we could expect growing demand over the coming years.”

“These are not new risks for the industry, but the interconnectedness of data centers across the economy means that the financial exposure can be significant. We understand that coverage is provided, but we would expect limits to be relatively modest, with exclusion regarding non-physical damage like power outage being standard. Also, the waiting period for business interruptions means that hyperscalers should be ready to cover the losses in the first hours or days.”

Operators will also need to consider less forgiving exposures when it comes to data centers. For example, as data centers increasingly become military targets as war infrastructure, as seen in the recent US-Iran war, operators may find themselves adrift with no coverage. For example, some reporting has suggested that Amazon Web Services data centers in Bahrain and the UAE that have been hit by drone strikes linked to Iran will not be able to claim insurance on their losses, as existing policies typically don’t cover war.

Standard property and cyber insurance policies generally contain war exclusions, with the insurer note required to pay out. This is obviously more of a problem in high-exposure zones, such as Ukraine and Eastern Europe, or Israel and the broader Middle East. And as these conflicts have become more of a problem for data centers, re/insurers have generally tightened war exclusion language and required explicit carve-outs.

## Cautious expansion

While the data center market continues to rapidly grow, insurers are cautiously expanding to match demand, creating a gap in insurance protection. Rapid construction timelines and large asset values will continue to be a mismatch with how the insurance sector operates, and S&P Global Ratings says insurers will maintain “strong underwriting discipline as they assess increasingly large and complex risks,” in the face of the pace of the industry.

Delpuech explains: “Because of this shortage of capacity, third-party capital outside of the insurance industry may be interested in covering the gap but this will require new innovative structures that make economic sense for all parties.”

The data center market is offering an immense opportunity for both investors and insurers, but where insurers are lagging, investors may follow suit. There already exist fears of an AI bubble. If it were to burst, it has the potential to be catastrophic to global markets, bigger than even the dot com bubble. The data center insurance industry is yet another example of an adjacent sector struggling under the pressure of the industry’s growth, as it builds the superstructure before the foundations are set.

If this insurance protection gap persists, investors in the industry might be less likely to throw all their eggs in one AI-shaped basket. And, given the magnitude of investment required to fund this industry, with some predicting around $3trn of required investment over the next five years, wavering now could spell disaster. Equally, as Delpuech argues, third-party capital may look to cover this gap and help to solve this issue, but as of yet those new and innovative structures are yet to be formed, and data center construction shows no signs of slowing.

stories.title: Digital Realty tops out second data center in Seoul, South Korea
stories.summary: Facility was first announced in 2021
stories.content:
The company this week announced the topping out of ICN11, its newest data center development in South Korea.

The facility is due to be operational by the second half of 2027.

“The topping out isn't just a construction milestone; it's a powerful symbol of what happens when incredible teams come together to build something bigger than any one of us could achieve alone,” the company said.

Plans for ICN11 (aka Digital Seoul 2) were first announced back in 2021, buying a land parcel in Gurae-dong, Gimpo City, in northwest Seoul. The 64MW facility is set to span almost 1 million sq ft (92,903 sqm). It was originally due to come online by the first half of 2023.

Digital currently operates its ICN10 (aka Digital Seoul 1) facility in Seoul. Announced in 2019 and live in 2022, the ten-story facility offers up to 12MW of IT capacity across 132,000 sq ft (12,265 sqm) of floorspace.

Digital is working with DPR Construction, DL E&C Co., Turner & Townsend, and Heerim Architects & Planners on the project.

stories.title: Pause in US data center construction could lead to recession, BlackRock CEO warns
stories.summary: Slowed buildout could turn massive investment into a massive crash
stories.content:
A pause in US data center construction could lead to a recession, the CEO of investment firm BlackRock has suggested.

In comments to CNBC, BlackRock CEO Larry Fink warned that a countrywide moratorium in the US will lead to a recession, with so much of the economy based on the buildout of the massive investments over the past few years in AI infrastructure.

Real estate services firm JLL said that forecasted data center capacity through 2030 will require $3 trillion in total investment. Demand remains high, with 97 percent global occupancy and 77 percent of the construction pipeline pre-committed to tenants, according to JLL.

In the US alone, competition for data center capacity is fierce, with demand now five times what it was two years ago and vacancy rates at one percent for three years in a row.

JLL says there remains clear investor confidence in the industry, with development accelerating to meet demand growth.

However, the US is also seeing significant opposition to data centers from local communities, government officials, and media. Multiple data center moratoriums are being considered or implemented up and down the country. Of those implemented, the shortest lasted just a week, and the longest will stretch up to a year and a half.

Even traditionally data center-friendly jurisdictions, such as Virginia, are looking into the effects of data centers on the local area, with Virginia's data center corridor, Loudoun County, voting to block new applications for facilities last month.

During the interview with CNBC, BlackRock’s Fink said that increasing opposition to data centers is mostly “misinformation,” arguing that data centers are creating “more new jobs than ever before.”

Moratoriums are just one log on the fire, however. There are significant issues that could lead to a delayed buildout of data centers in the US. Discussions around energy costs and grid upgrades, for example, have dominated discourse in the US and are far from finished.

The industry’s explosive growth has also led to shortages in the supply of equipment, raw materials, and labor, which are leading to delays in project delivery globally.

stories.title: Meta named as company behind 3,000 acre data center project in Mason County, Kentucky
stories.summary: Will receive a 40-year tax break on property taxes
stories.content:
Meta has been named as the company looking to develop almost 3,000 acres into a data center campus in Mason County.

As per a report from the Ledger Independent, Meta was identified during an October 13 Mason County Fiscal Court meeting, in which a community benefits agreement was passed by county commissioners.

Under that agreement, Meta will invest $10 billion in the project, with the potential for this to grow in future phases, and will generate more than 4,000 construction jobs and 300 long-term roles once operational. Meta will also contribute $115 million to infrastructure improvements on roads, water treatment plants, and pipelines and will see annual payments to the county in the millions of dollars per development phase.

In return, Meta has been awarded a 40-year tax break on local property taxes - there will be $800bn in Industrial Revenue Bonds (IRBs) for this project, with an estimated $10 billion per phase.

That a massive data center campus was coming to the area was first revealed in November 2025, with an anonymous developer at the time evaluating 5,000 acres of land near the Big Pond and Tuckahoe roads.

In May of this year, a 2,080-acre parcel in the area was rezoned for data center use, with documents suggesting six 718,740 sq ft (66,773 sqm) data center buildings and three substations would be built at the site. Power capacity has been said to possibly reach up to 2.2GW.

The local community has voiced concerns regarding the project, with a petition against the project having 1,429 signatures at the time of writing.

Meta said: “We’re grateful to the Mason County fiscal court for its careful review. With this potential project, we’ll not only pay the full cost of the power we use, but we’ll invest directly in Mason County — in schools, workforce training and local infrastructure — guided by what local leaders and residents tell us they need. We take seriously the diversity of opinions in the county, and we intend to keep showing up and listening, not just during the approval process but in the long run.”

Mason County Judge Executive Owen McNeill added: “This agreement with Meta represents the hard work of many dedicated individuals and organizations that envisioned a brighter future for Mason County and all of our residents. Meta represents the pinnacle of technology companies that only a few short years ago, we would have never dreamt would invest here. For our community, closer to the rural end of the spectrum than urban, their investments positively address just about every issue our communities are facing today and will greatly bolster them well into the future.”

stories.title: Greece drafts legislation requiring data centers source 60% of power from renewables
stories.summary: Also proposes the creation of a data center registry
stories.content:
The Greek government has proposed new legislation that could require data centers to source at least 60 percent of their power from renewable sources.

The Ministry of Environment and Energy proposed the draft legislation, which also includes several other provisions seeking to set stricter requirements for data centers.

These include requiring data center investors to reserve grid capacity only when they can prove sufficient financial backing and investment readiness, and requiring them to cover grid connection and related grid reinforcement costs.

The rules would also render data centers subject to financial capacity checks, including turnover criteria for projects connecting to the transmission system. In addition, data centers seeking a connection would have to provide a €200,000 ($224,089) per MW bank guarantee to prevent speculative applications from entering the grid connection queue.

In addition, the draft legislation proposed that the Regulatory Authority for Waste, Energy and Water (RAAEY) create a data center registry to track developments in the sector and improve transparency.

The draft legislation also includes the introduction of flexible grid connection agreements in locations with insufficient capacity, which will permit grid operators to limit the amount of power a facility can draw from the grid within set limits. In addition, the legislation proposes that transmission and distribution operators publish information every three months on available connection capacity by region.

Finally, the proposals set out the establishment of a €2.3 billion ($2.57bn) Island Decarbonization Fund to finance projects that would reduce reliance on oil-fired generation in favor of renewable energy and storage facilities.

The consultation will last until October 24, 2026.

The draft legislation follows Spain, which proposed new legislation in August that would require data centers to source at least 80 percent of their electricity consumption from new renewable generation on an hourly basis.

Greece is a relatively small data center market compared to the rest of Europe, but has seen significant expansion over recent years. According to Data Center Map, the country currently has 29 operational facilities across 19 operators. Digital Realty launched its first data center in the country in April of last year on the island of Crete.

This would have been the country’s first digital infrastructure real estate investment trust (REIT) listing if offerred in 4Q 2026, its original […]
stories.content:
Philippines telco PLDT Inc. has postponed the public listing of its data center unit Vitro REIT Inc. to 2027 citing unfavourable market conditions amid rising interest rates, the firm said in an exchange filing recently. This would have been the country’s first digital infrastructure real estate investment trust (REIT) listing if offerred in 4Q 2026, its original target period.

“In light of current market conditions and rising interest rates, Vitro REIT has decided to defer the IPO to 2027. PLDT remains committed to the proposed VITRO REIT IPO as an important part of the Group’s asset monetization and deleveraging plans, while supporting expansion of the REIT portfolio and continued growth of the Group’s data center business,” it said. No further details of the next possible target date was given.

In June, <u>w.media</u> reported on the proposed listing which was expected to raise as much as US$ 400 million. The IPO would include VITRO REIT’s portfolio of eight Tier 2 and Tier 3 data center assets totaling 24MW.

The Philippines central bank has raised interest rates three times this year while headline inflation has risen to 7.2 per cent in September from 6.1 per cent in August, the fastest in three years. The Philippines stock market has seen a sea of red with foreign investors being net sellers. This comes on the back of high oil prices, a weak peso and high Treasury yields.

stories.title: Oracle renews attempts to secure natural gas pipeline approval for Project Jupiter data center - report
stories.summary: Seeks approval from FERC to expedite approval of the 17.8-mile pipeline
stories.content:
Oracle has revived attempts to secure approval for a natural gas pipeline extension needed to feed its 2.5GW Project Jupiter data center campus in Doña Ana County, New Mexico.

According to Bloomberg, the cloud computing firm asked the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) to expedite approval of the 17.8-mile (28.6km) Green Chile pipeline, which would transport about 400 million cubic feet of natural gas daily to on-site fuel cells that will power the facility. Bloom Energy is supplying the fuel cells and has signed several offtake deals with other data center firms.

In a letter to FERC, the company said that the development is projected to support nearly 5,800 peak construction jobs and generate up to $1.1 billion in annual economic output for the local county.

In July, Energy Transfer, a midstream gas firm, saw its application to build a new natural gas pipeline to feed the site rejected by state regulators. State officials cited large-scale water use, increased CO2 emissions, and a lack of state revenue generation as major factors in their decision.

Despite the rejection, Oracle said the project remained on schedule. However, in September, it was reported that the company had sent a force majeure notice to Blue Owl Capital in an effort to shield itself from potential increased costs should the facility fail to come online in 2028 as planned, which would allow the firm to delay the payments it would have to make, rather than forfeit its tenancy.

With the pipeline's operational timeline now set for February 2027, well past its August target, there is growing trepidation that the data center could also face significant delays.

In response to the renewed push for approval, environmental groups and the state's attorney general, Raúl Torrez, have sought to pressure FERC to broaden its environmental review, asking the agency to evaluate the combined footprint of the data center and the pipeline before granting approval.

As a workaround for its gas supply issues, recent reports revealed that the company has been trucking in compressed natural gas to its Salt Lake City and Texas data centers for the past year. According to the reports, the company is now considering the same model for the Project Jupiter data center.

stories.title: Odisha Cabinet greenlights US$ 18.62 million backup data center
stories.summary: The Odisha Cabinet in India has approved a Rs 176.83 crore (US$ 18.62 million) disaster recovery data center, set to be built on the south campus of Dharanidhar University in Keonjhar district. According to ET Datacenters, the disaster recovery data center will function as a geographically separate backup and recovery center for the state’s primary […]
stories.content:
The Odisha Cabinet in India has approved a Rs 176.83 crore (US$ 18.62 million) disaster recovery data center, set to be built on the south campus of Dharanidhar University in Keonjhar district.

According to ET Datacenters, the disaster recovery data center will function as a geographically separate backup and recovery center for the state’s primary data center in Bhubaneswar. In the event of major technical failures, cyberattacks, or natural disasters, the new facility would be able to restore essential government digital services.

The facility will have its own independent power supply, cooling systems, connectivity, and computing infrastructure. The goal is to allow the facility to operate as a recovery site with no reliance on the primary data center’s infrastructure.

Of the total cost, Rs 154 crore (US$ 16.22 million) has been allocated for capital expenditure, with the remaining Rs 22.83 crore (US$ 2.4 million) reserved for operational expenditure over a five-year period. The Fifth State Finance Commission has provided a grant-in-aid of Rs 162.83 crore (US$ 17.15 million) for the project. The balance will be covered by the Odisha Computer Application Centre, which will draw from the Electronics and Information Technology Department’s State Data Centre maintenance budget.

The state has set a nine-month implementation period, followed by five years of operations and maintenance. Krystal Integrated Services Limited has been selected to assist with the project.

The Odisha State Data Centre (OSDC), in Bhubaneswar has been operational since 2011 and hosts applications essential to the state and its departments. In July, Odisha TV reported that as demand for digital infrastructure rose, an upgrade was necessary. The state government has approved the establishment of Odisha State Data Centre 2.0 with a total approved cost of Rs 268.44 crore (US$ 28.29 million).

stories.title: Ukrainian drones strike Sberbank data center under construction in Russia
stories.summary: Ukrainian drones have struck a data center under construction for Russian state lender Sberbank in Balakovo, Saratov region, overnight on October 14, killing one woman and damaging several residential buildings. Alexander Vedyakhin, First Deputy CEO, Sberbank, confirmed the attack, saying the bank’s systems and online services continued to operate normally. The bank also said no […]
stories.content:
Ukrainian drones have struck a data center under construction for Russian state lender Sberbank in Balakovo, Saratov region, overnight on October 14, killing one woman and damaging several residential buildings.

Alexander Vedyakhin, First Deputy CEO, Sberbank, confirmed the attack, saying the bank’s systems and online services continued to operate normally. The bank also said no employees were injured as reported by The Moscow Times.

However, users across Russia reported disruptions to Sberbank’s services such as its GigaChat AI platform and other major online services, according to outage tracker Detector404. No link between the reported disruptions and the drone attack was established.

Roman Busargin, Governor, Saratov region, told Meduza all infrastructure facilities in the city were “operating normally” without specifically identifying the data center as a target.

Readers will recall that the strike follows Ukrainian drone attacks last week on data centers belonging to Russian technology company Yandex in the Ryazan, Vladimir and Kaluga regions.

stories.title: Data centre investors must bear necessary grid upgrade costs, says Johari Ghani
stories.summary: Malaysia wants data centre investors to bear the cost of transmission upgrades required by their projects rather than pass the investment to the local players.

sources.name: The Edge Malaysia — data centre search

stories.content:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 15): Malaysia wants data centre investors to bear the cost of transmission upgrades required by their projects rather than pass the investment to the local players.

The infrastructure costs should form part of investors’ project expenditure, with Tenaga Nasional Bhd (KL:TENAGA) advising on the upgrades needed, Minister of Investment, Trade and Industry Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani told the Dewan Rakyat during question time on Thursday.

“This is our strategy to ensure that economic activities that existed before the arrival of data centres are not adversely affected,” he said.

Johari was responding to Ampang MP Rodziah Ismail (PH-PKR), who asked how the government measures data centres’ net economic contribution after accounting for their use of electricity, water, land and infrastructure, as well as incentives and the opportunity cost of national resources.

A wave of energy-intensive data centres has been surging across Malaysia amid a global boom in artificial intelligence. Tenaga Nasional, the country’s national electric utility firm, is now supplying power to 36 data centres with dozens more in the pipeline.

Johari also said data centre operators would be charged for electricity capacity committed to them even if they did not fully use it, to prevent capacity being tied up without compensation. He cited an operator securing 200 megawatts but using only half of the capacity once its facility was ready.

“The other 100MW that you do not use, we assume you have used it,” he said. “We charge you. That is our policy now.” Tenaga Nasional could not freely reallocate the unused capacity because it remained committed to meeting the operator’s future requirements, Johari explained.

All electricity requirements for data centres should also be treated separately from those of households and other industries, without subsidies, and where generation relies on gas, its market price should be reflected in the cost of supplying the data centre, Johari said.

The aim is to protect the reserve capacity needed for other economic activities, he noted.

Further, the government now wants data centre investments to generate more opportunities for Malaysian suppliers, engineers, technicians and universities.

A task force on data centres had agreed on a minimum 30% local content level, with greater domestic participation in construction, engineering services, cooling systems and electrical equipment.

Johari also called for Malaysian companies and universities to have access to data centres’ computing capacity for research and development, rather than allowing their benefits to accrue primarily to overseas customers.

“We want our people to be able to access the technology,” he said, adding that collaboration with universities could help Malaysia develop its own capabilities over time.

Deputy Minister Abdul Rahman Mohamad suggested that operators consider developing their own power generation and water supply. A planned 1 GW hybrid energy project by UEM Lestra could enhance Johor’s electricity supply and reduce inter-state dependence.

stories.title: CapitaLand India Trust unveils US$203.2 million Chennai data centre
stories.summary: The 53 MW facility is due for completion by end-2026

sources.name: The Business Times — Data Centres topic

stories.content:
The 53 MW facility is due for completion by end-2026

\[SINGAPORE\] has launched a new data centre in Chennai entailing an investment of about 19.4 billion rupees (US$203.2 million), even as its sponsor and manager expands its digital infrastructure footprint in India.

CapitaLand Data Centre Chennai 01, Clint’s first data-centre development in the state of Tamil Nadu, will have a gross power capacity of 53 megawatts (MW) when completed by the end of 2026.

The project was launched on Thursday (Oct 15) by Singapore Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Energy, Trade and Industry (Trade) Gan Kim Yong and the chief minister of Tamil Nadu, C Joseph Vijay.

Located in Ambattur, an established data-centre corridor in Chennai, the development is jointly held by Clint and CapitaLand India Data Centre Fund.

The facility will have 34 MW of power capacity for information technology equipment across 13 data halls. It is designed to support high-density computing systems, including those using liquid cooling, and offer customers a choice of network providers.

The CEO of Clint’s manager, Gauri Shankar Nagabhushanam, said: “The development reflects our conviction in the long-term growth of India’s data-centre sector, and is designed to meet the evolving requirements of hyperscale and enterprise customers.”

The Chennai project follows Clint’s data-centre development in Navi Mumbai, which has been fully leased to a leading global hyperscaler.

CLI said it intends to continue expanding its data centre, logistics and industrial portfolio in Tamil Nadu through its listed and private fund platforms.

The group has operated in the state for 22 years and has invested more than 60 billion rupees in seven operational assets.

Its Tamil Nadu portfolio encompasses business parks, industrial and logistics facilities, lodging and digital infrastructure. CLI first entered the state through International Tech Park Chennai in 2004.

CLI India chief executive Quaiser Parvez said the group is positioned to support Tamil Nadu’s growth as a technology, manufacturing and digital economy hub through its investment, development and fund-management capabilities.

India is a core market for CLI. Its funds under management in the country exceeded S$8 billion as at Jun 30.

Its India portfolio comprises nine business parks, 14 industrial and logistics properties, four data centres under development and three co-working spaces.

Its lodging arm, , manages about 6,300 units in 24 operating and pipeline hotels and serviced residences in India.

stories.content:
Brightray Science Inc, a majority-owned subsidiary of BUUU Group Limited, has announced that its wholly owned subsidiary Brightray Veridian Pte. Ltd. has signed a letter of intent (LOI) with an unnamed US-based mission-critical infrastructure partner for a planned 10 MW AI data center project in Indiana, United States.

This is, according to a press release, Brightray’s first project LOI signed in the US and an important step toward expanding into the world’s largest data center market. Under the LOI, Brightray will deploy a prefabricated data center solution. The implementation is subject to final agreement on technical specifications, commercial terms, the project schedule, and definitive contract documentation.

“Entering the US market is an important step in Brightray’s international development. The US has enormous data center demand, and customers face real pressure to turn their AI investments into usable computing power as quickly as possible. Our entry point is delivery: with Brightray prefabricated data center solution, we move more of the work into the factory and run manufacturing in parallel with on-site works, with the aim of shortening the delivery period for this project to within one year,” said Bin Wang, Brightray founder.

By taking this approach, Brightray says it can deliver the 10 MW AI data center within a year. That timeline covers the entire schedule, including design finalization, permitting, international shipping, on-site foundation and ancillary works, installation, and commissioning.

“We look forward to working further with our partner on the technical solution and implementation arrangements and to building delivery experience in the US market through this 10MW project. Addressing the power, cooling and space requirements of next-generation AI equipment, we aim to bring the efficiency advantages of our prefabricated data center solution to the project and lay the foundation for the further expansion of our US business,” said Wang.

If this agreement is finalized and the project delivered, it could serve as a blueprint for Brightray’s expansion into the US market.

Grid capacity constraints, community opposition, and infrastructure bottlenecks can significantly delay data center buildouts in the US market, a problem Brightray looks to want to solve. Despite the constraints, US data center investments have nearly doubled since 2024, according to Arizton Advisory & Intelligence, and demand for AI will only push that growth higher with the US data center market expected to be worth US$ 494.49 billion by 2031.

stories.content:
Submer India Private Limited, part of the Submer Group, has signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) with BSNL Tower Corporation Limited (BTCL). The collaboration will focus on infrastructure designed for the growing requirements of artificial intelligence (AI) and high-performance computing.
### Key Areas of Assessment

The parties will jointly assess opportunities for GPU-as-a-Service, Sovereign AI cloud infrastructure, and edge and micro-edge data centers. They will also evaluate large-scale data center projects of up to 20 MW.BSNL premises and data center facilities will be assessed for transformation into distributed edge infrastructure. He added that the next step is to build the physical capacity to turn that ambition into deployable compute.Submer will apply its expertise in integrated data center architecture, liquid cooling, thermal management, and high-density computing. Cooling, power, facilities, and IT infrastructure will be considered as one system from the outset.This approach will help the parties assess infrastructure designed for the density and efficiency requirements of modern AI. BTCL will coordinate access to relevant BSNL premises and data center facilities for feasibility studies.It will also support connectivity, regulatory alignment, and engagement with government and enterprise stakeholders. stories.title: DayOne lifts Malaysia financing to USD $7.2 billion
stories.summary: The enlarged package will fund Johor data centre expansion as billed capacity passes 1GW and bookings climb to 2.3GW.
stories.content:
Thu, 15th Oct 2026 (Yesterday)
DayOne has increased its Malaysia financing to about USD $7.2 billion and said its billings have passed 1GW. The funding will support its data centre platform in Johor.

The Singapore-headquartered group said the enlarged senior secured multi-currency syndicated term financing was arranged by a seven-lender consortium. It follows roughly USD $3.5 billion of syndicated financing secured in May 2025 for the same Johor platform.

Alongside the financing update, DayOne said bookings reached about 2.3GW, up from 1.25GW at the end of 2025. It also reported 1.1GW of reservations from customers under legally binding contracts.

DayOne defines billings as income-generating IT power capacity under long-term customer contracts that remain in effect. On that basis, billed capacity has risen more than eightfold in less than two years, from 121MW at the end of 2024 to more than 1GW.

### Johor expansion

The financing marks another major commitment to Johor, which has become one of Southeast Asia's main locations for data centre development. Operators have been drawn to the Malaysian state by available land, proximity to Singapore, and rising demand from cloud and artificial intelligence workloads.

DayOne said it has raised more than USD $6 billion in equity since 2024 through several funding rounds. It also has project financing support from more than 30 local and international banking partners.

The company operates across 10 markets in Asia Pacific and Europe, including Singapore, several locations in Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand, Japan, Hong Kong, Finland, and Spain.

Its total resources, which include in-service capacity, capacity under construction, and secured powered land, stood at 4.6GW, compared with 2GW at the end of 2025.

### Customer base

Growth in bookings has also come with a broader customer roster. Bookings came from 15 customers, compared with nine at the end of 2024.

Four of its five largest customers are present with the company in more than one market. It also said three hyperscale customers each have multi-market deployments of around or above 200MW.

DayOne recently secured additional orders from an existing US hyperscale customer. It did not name the customer or disclose the value of the latest order.

Data centre operators and investors have been racing to secure power, land, and financing as demand rises for facilities built to support AI training and cloud services. In that environment, contracted power capacity has become a closely watched indicator because it reflects both customer demand and an operator's ability to bring new sites into service.

Johor has benefited from that trend as developers expand beyond Singapore, where land and power constraints have shaped growth. For operators with campuses on both sides of the border, the area offers a way to serve regional demand while staying close to Singapore's connectivity and customer base.

Jamie Khoo, Chief Executive Officer of DayOne, said: "The confidence our banking partners and customers have placed in DayOne is reflected in these milestones and underpins our continued growth. Together, their support has enabled us to unlock strategic capacity for the next generation of AI and cloud infrastructure. Our focus remains on earning that trust through responsible execution and bringing capacity online at speed and scale in the markets our customers need."

Khoo also set out the company's view on its expansion into new regions.

"By pioneering and scaling new markets, this conviction has shaped DayOne since inception, and it continues to guide how we grow," Khoo said. "From Singapore, where DayOne was founded, we are driving the delivery of high-specification facilities across Asia Pacific and Europe."
